references.text: Joseph himself dreams a dream that plays an important role in God's plan, paralleling the dreams of the cupbearer and the baker in prison.
Joseph's second dream reinforces the theme that God uses dreams to reveal the future, just as he does for Joseph's fellow prisoners.
God speaks to Abimelech in a dream at night, an early example in Genesis of God communicating through dreams.
Joseph explains that interpretations belong to God, emphasizing the divine origin of the dreams mentioned in verse 5.
Pharaoh dreams two dreams that Joseph later interprets, a direct continuation of the theme of divine revelation through dreams.
Reference to Joseph's time in prison where the Lord's word tested him until what he had predicted came to pass.
God declares that he reveals himself to prophets through visions and speaks to them in dreams, an important theological background for the dreams in Genesis 40:5.
King Nebuchadnezzar dreams dreams that predict the future, parallel to the dreams in prison which also contain divine messages about the future.
This is a direct retelling of the same event where the meaning of the dreams becomes clear through Joseph's interpretation.
